BLOCKING OSCILLATOR
These circuits produce non-sine wave outputs. The blocking oscillator produces narrow pulses while the sawtooth generator produces sawtooth shaped pulses.
The sawtooth generator must have a square wave input signal to produce an output signal.
An incorrect output waveform indicates that the circuit is faulted.
Let's begin the lesson on NON-SINE WAVE OSCILLATOR TROUBLESHOOTING EXPERIMENT.
LESSON MENU
NON-SINE WAVE OSC. FAULTS
Although the two circuits below produce outputs other than a sine wave, they are very different.
DISCUSSION
The blocking oscillator uses a transformer and capacitor in a feedback circuit. It continually produces output pulses.
The sawtooth generator has no feedback circuit. It is not capable of producing an output signal by itself. An external input is required.
Obviously, different troubleshooting techniques are required, however, the principles are the same as other transistor circuits.
Let's begin the troubleshooting discussion with the blocking oscillator.
To determine correct operation of a blocking oscillator, simply measure the output with an oscilloscope and vary any frequency determining components.

In this sawtooth generator, the output waveform is generated by the charging and rapid discharging of C2 or C3, selected by S1.
If the capacitor shorts, the output is grounded and the signal drops to zero. This fault can be verified by measuring from TP4 to TP1 (ground).
If the capacitor opens, no charge or discharge occurs. The output is a square wave, just like the input. With C2 open, the circuit is a simple amplifier.
An open capacitor is impossible to detect with an ohmmeter. If the output is ever a square wave, replace the capacitor, and recheck the circuit.
When repaired, always verify correct operation. These procedures will allow you to locate many of the common faults associated with sawtooth generators.
